overview: Skellerup is a New Zealand-headquartered (founded 115 years ago) global designer and manufacturer of engineered polymer and rubber products, operating through two divisions: Agri (dairy rubberware consumables and Red Band/Skellerup-branded footwear) and Industrial (technical seals, gaskets and vacuum systems for potable water/wastewater, roofing/construction, mining, automotive and other applications). Almost 90% of what it sells is moulded or extruded polymer. The group manufactures at its own and partner facilities in New Zealand, Australia, China, Vietnam, the UK, Europe (Netherlands) and the US, and sold to over 3,700 customers in 87+ countries in FY2025, with more than 80% of revenue earned offshore (North America ~37-40% of group revenue is the single largest market).

business_model.summary: Two-segment industrial manufacturer: Agri sells largely consumable, replacement-cycle dairy rubberware (milking liners, tubing, teats, Clip-On/Ultraliner-type products) plus Red Band/specialty footwear, sold via both OEM (milking-platform manufacturers) and Skellerup-branded channels; Industrial sells technical, specification-critical polymer components (seals/gaskets for potable water and wastewater pipe networks, roofing/construction membranes and flashings, vacuum pump systems, marine foam, automotive/mining components) mostly to OEM and distributor/contractor channels in the US, Australia, UK/Europe and Asia. FY2025 group revenue NZ$353.5m split roughly Industrial $241.3m (68%) / Agri $112.2m (32%); H1 FY2026 revenue $183.5m split Industrial $122.6m (67%) / Agri $61.4m (33%). Agri carries materially higher segment margins (FY25 Agri EBIT margin ~31% vs Industrial ~20%) because dairy consumables are replaced on a routine cycle largely independent of farmer capex decisions, giving Agri a demand profile closer to a consumable than to a discretionary capital good.

revenue_streams.name: Industrial - Potable Water & Wastewater
revenue_streams.note: share of Industrial division revenue, FY25; largest and fastest-growing Industrial application, notably in the US

revenue_streams.name: Industrial - Roofing & Construction
revenue_streams.note: share of Industrial division revenue, FY25; UK solar and North American roofing strong, Australasia soft

revenue_streams.name: Agri - Dairy rubberware
revenue_streams.note: share of Agri division revenue, FY25 (80% in H1 FY26); milking liners, tubing, teats, OEM and branded

revenue_streams.name: Agri - Footwear
revenue_streams.note: share of Agri division revenue, FY25; Red Band/Skellerup brand plus growing US specialty/utility footwear, margin pressured by raw material costs

revenue_streams.name: Industrial - Other (automotive/machinery, mining, sport & leisure, electrical, health & hygiene)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - OEM manufacturers (milking-platform makers, industrial equipment builders), distributors/wholesalers, and direct branded sales into dairy farms and industrial/construction contractors; not B2C in any material way despite consumer-recognisable Red Band brand (sold through retail/rural-supply channels)
business_model.geographic_mix: H1 FY2026 group revenue by market: North America ~38-40%, New Zealand ~11-20% (higher in Agri), Australia ~15-18%, Europe ~10-19%, Asia ~3-12%, UK & Ireland ~7-9%. Industrial skews more North American and globally diversified; Agri skews more North America/New Zealand/Europe. Manufacturing footprint: New Zealand (Wigram, Christchurch - largest site), China (Jiangsu), Vietnam (major third-party contract manufacturing partner), Australia, UK, Netherlands (new distribution facility opened April 2025), US.

main_competitors: GEA Farm Technologies (dairy equipment, adjacent OEM/competitor)
Various regional gasket, seal and roofing-membrane manufacturers in the US, Europe and Asia (fragmented Industrial competitive set)
Generic/lower-cost Asian rubberware and footwear manufacturers (price competition in footwear and commodity seals)
competitive_position.market_position: Global leader (management's own characterisation) in dairy rubberware consumable design and manufacture; a smaller, specification-driven niche player within the much larger and more fragmented global market for engineered polymer seals, gaskets and vacuum systems used in water infrastructure, roofing and construction

moat_factors.description: Products must meet stringent food-grade, drinking-water, hygiene and safety standards and pass lengthy industry testing/approval processes; once a component is specified into an OEM's platform (milking systems, potable water infrastructure) or approved by a water authority, switching costs for the customer are high

Milking liners, tubing and teats are routinely replaced on a defined cycle for hygiene/food-safety reasons independent of farmer capex cycles, giving Agri revenue a demand floor even when farmer capital spending is weak

Red Band is an iconic, trusted New Zealand consumer brand in gumboots/footwear; Skellerup and Masport (vacuum pumps) carry technical reputation with OEM customers, but the group is not brand-led outside NZ footwear and dairy

Deep material science and multi-material integration capability (Product Development Centres) lets Skellerup rapidly prototype and win new OEM specification wins (management cites this repeatedly as the key differentiator vs competitors, e.g. Masport hydro-excavation win, high-pressure potable water gasket)
Growth from new OEM products typically requires little incremental capex because customers/manufacturing partners co-invest, supporting high incremental margins and low reinvestment needs
Multi-country footprint (NZ, China, Vietnam, UK, US) gives some flexibility to shift production in response to tariffs/freight/FX, though this is a partial mitigant, not a true structural moat

weaknesses: No single dominant global scale advantage in Industrial - it competes against much larger diversified conglomerates (Trelleborg and others) in a fragmented market where Skellerup is a niche player
Footwear sub-segment is more commoditised, exposed to raw material cost inflation and Asian manufacturing competition, and has been a drag on Agri margins in some years

Customer concentration risk at the individual-site level (e.g. a single Health & Hygiene customer pausing production to relocate assembly cut H1 FY2026 Industrial revenue in that application; a single Asia customer production pause similarly hit results)

Reliance on a major third-party contract manufacturing partner in Vietnam for a substantial share of Agri/other production introduces counterparty and quality-control risk outside Skellerup's own facilities
Small absolute size (~NZ$390m FY2026 revenue) limits ability to match larger competitors' R&D and capex spending in absolute dollar terms

growth_drivers: Continued new-product wins with global OEM customers in both Agri (Thriver calf-feeding range, Evolution SST-Driver recyclable-shell liner, new high-performance milking liners launched in the US) and Industrial (hydro-excavation vacuum systems, high-pressure potable water gaskets, roofing/solar products) - management states >440 new products taken to market in the 24 months to FY25

US and European market expansion, including the new Netherlands distribution/conversion facility (opened April 2025) supporting U-DEK marine foam and other Industrial sales into Europe, and continued growth of North America as a share of group revenue (up to ~38-40% of H1 FY26 revenue)

New direct China presence for dairy consumables and continued in-market capability build-out (management flagged the next 12-36 months from FY25 as a potential 'watershed period' for configuring the business, including possible in-market manufacturing investment)

Capacity and productivity investment at the core Wigram (Christchurch) dairy rubberware facility - new moulding/rubber processing equipment commissioned in FY25, and a replacement continuous-vulcanisation (CV) line to be installed/commissioned by end of FY2027 following the August 2025 fire

Potable water and wastewater infrastructure demand, a structurally growing, less-cyclical Industrial application (ageing pipe networks, water security investment) - the single largest and fastest-growing Industrial application in FY25/H1 FY26
Roofing & construction growth from solar installation demand in the UK and improving Asia/Australia markets, offsetting a soft Australasian general construction cycle
Global protein/dairy demand growth (management cites industry estimates of 3-8% per annum food-protein demand growth) supporting long-run Agri volumes

Disciplined M&A optionality funded by strong operating cash flow and very low leverage (net debt fell to <NZ$2m by FY2026 year-end) - management explicitly looks for bolt-on acquisitions that extend capability, market application or geographic footprint, though it has stated it will not deviate from tight return parameters

Management's own stated medium-term target of 11-12% compound annual EBIT/earnings growth (cited on the FY2026 results call), consistent with the group's nine (FY25) and now ten (FY26) consecutive years of record EBIT

business.risk: NZ/global dairy cycle and Fonterra payout exposure
business.description: Agri (~30% of group revenue) is linked to global dairy farmer economics; while consumable rubberware demand is less capex-sensitive than dairy equipment sales, footwear and discretionary farm spending can soften in weak payout years. Fonterra's forecast Farmgate Milk Price has been volatile through FY2026 - the 2025/26 season settled at $9.60-$9.80/kgMS (near-record) but the 2026/27 forecast was subsequently cut by Fonterra to $9.25/kgMS (from $9.75) in mid-2026 on softer global dairy prices, a signal of potential moderation in farmer sentiment/spending into FY2027

Individual large OEM or distribution customers pausing production or relocating (e.g. a Health & Hygiene customer's assembly relocation, and a separate Asia production pause) have had visible, quantifiable revenue impacts in single reporting periods, illustrating vulnerability to lumpy customer decisions despite a broad 3,700+ customer base

Roofing & construction (~16% of FY25 group revenue by application) is exposed to the building cycle; Australasian construction was explicitly called out as soft in both FY25 and H1 FY26, partially offset by UK/US strength

A significant share of production (including footwear and some Agri/Industrial componentry) runs through a major contract manufacturing partner in Vietnam; management explicitly cites the need for frequent staff travel to monitor quality/production there, and Vietnam is separately a focal point of US tariff policy

SKL.NZ (cross-listed SKL.AX) is a small-cap industrial (~NZ$1.2bn market cap as of mid-2026); trading liquidity is thinner than large-cap peers, which can widen bid/ask spreads and amplify price moves on news

CEO transition already occurred (David Mair to Graham Leaming, effective 1 April 2024); Leaming has now delivered two full annual results (FY25, FY26) demonstrating continuity, but the business is still relatively early in the new CEO's tenure and Chair John Strowger has flagged the next 12-36 months (from FY25) as a strategically significant 'watershed' period requiring careful capital deployment execution

financial.description: More than 80% of group revenue is earned in international markets (predominantly USD, EUR, AUD, GBP) and translated back into NZD reporting currency; the FY26 NPAT bridge explicitly showed an 'unfavourable FX result from unfavourable FX revaluations and hedging losses' as a drag on H1 FY26 earnings, even though a weaker NZD is a translation tailwind embedded within each application's reported growth. The Board also noted rising imputation credits reflect 'the increasing proportion of Skellerup's growth in profit being earned overseas', implying growing exposure to offshore tax/FX dynamics

Modest given very low absolute debt levels (net debt fell from NZ$20.4m at Dec-2024 to NZ$17.5m at Dec-2025 to under NZ$2m by FY26 year-end, against a NZ$55m syndicated multi-currency facility with ANZ/ASB expiring August 2028); finance costs are a small line item and have been declining as debt is paid down

financial.risk: Raw material and freight cost inflation
financial.description: Synthetic/natural rubber and polymer input costs, plus freight, have repeatedly been cited as margin pressure points - explicitly flagged as eroding footwear EBIT growth in both FY25 and H1 FY26, and as a factor Industrial gross margin had to absorb alongside tariffs and freight cost increases 'which could not be fully recovered' in FY25

regulatory.description: This is the single most material and actively disclosed risk. Skellerup generates ~37-40% of group revenue from the US market, and approximately 85% of that US-market revenue is sourced from products manufactured at facilities in New Zealand, China and Vietnam (in roughly equal proportion, per the FY25 Chair's Review). Management disclosed working assumptions of incremental tariff rates of up to 30% on China-origin goods, 20% on Vietnam-origin goods and 15% on NZ-origin goods (FY25 annual report), later described as reduced to a 'substantially lower' ~12.5% blended regime by the FY26 results call. The company mitigated FY25/H1 FY26 impact via pre-emptive inventory build, pricing actions, cost initiatives and product/manufacturing mix shifts, quantifying incremental net tariff costs of ~NZ$0.7m (Industrial) and ~NZ$0.3m (Agri) in H1 FY26 alone. Management stated it expects to fully offset tariffs on a run-rate basis entering FY2027, but explicitly cautions that 'the final outcome of tariff negotiations... is unknown' and 'the position appears to change every week' - the situation remains fluid and could deteriorate again

The Group's climate disclosures flag that a quarter of Group revenue (dairy) is consumable in nature, and future waste-recovery/recycling regulation could raise the cost of servicing that market; Skellerup is proactively developing liner recovery/recyclable-shell programmes (e.g. Evolution SST-Driver) partly to get ahead of anticipated regulation

Skellerup is a mandatory NZ climate reporting entity (Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, Part 7A); compliance costs are recurring but management assesses financial/physical climate risk exposure of material assets as 0% at moderate-or-above rating in current scenarios - not currently a material earnings risk

macro.risk: Global economic/political uncertainty depressing OEM capex decisions
macro.description: FY25 annual report explicitly noted some Industrial OEM customer development projects were delayed and other customers paused investment decisions in response to 'geo-political unpredictability'; management's FY2026 outlook language repeatedly references 'global geopolitical uncertainty' making forecasting difficult

See Fonterra payout discussion above; a sustained downturn in global dairy prices would eventually flow through to farmer capex and, to a lesser extent, consumable replacement discipline, even though liners/tubing are largely non-discretionary for food-safety compliance

COVID-19 and regional conflicts (Middle East conflict cited in FY26 commentary) have previously interrupted freight routes and sourcing; the Group holds elevated inventory levels partly as a buffer against this

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Skellerup sits across two structurally distinct end markets: (1) global dairy/protein demand, which industry estimates put at 3-8% per annum long-run growth, underpinning steady Agri consumable volumes; and (2) global water/wastewater infrastructure investment and construction/roofing activity, which is more cyclical but has a long-run structural tailwind from ageing infrastructure replacement and water security investment, particularly in North America
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate and asymmetric across segments - Agri dairy rubberware behaves more like a non-discretionary consumable (food-safety driven replacement cycle) with lower cyclicality; Industrial (roofing/construction, automotive/machinery, mining) is more exposed to the general industrial/construction cycle, though potable water/wastewater within Industrial is itself fairly defensive (essential infrastructure spend)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity given minimal net debt (<NZ$2m at FY2026 year-end against a NZ$55m facility); indirect sensitivity via customer capex decisions (farmer investment, OEM/construction capex) is more relevant than the company's own funding cost
key_input_costs: Labour (815 people worldwide as of H1 FY26)

recent_developments.event: FY2025 record results: revenue NZ$353.5m (+7%), EBIT NZ$78.0m (+7%, ninth consecutive record year), statutory NPAT NZ$54.5m (underlying +9%), EPS 27.8cps, DPS 25.5cps (92% payout ratio), net debt down to NZ$12.4m. Management disclosed detailed tariff exposure (37% of revenue from US, ~85% of that from NZ/China/Vietnam-manufactured product) and mitigation strategy

Fire damaged one of two continuous vulcanisation (CV) lines at the Wigram (Christchurch) facility, Skellerup's largest manufacturing site; operations continued on the single remaining CV line while a replacement was planned
New Skellerup distribution/conversion facility opened in the Netherlands to support European growth (notably U-DEK marine foam products)

Record H1 FY26 half-year: revenue NZ$183.5m (+11%), EBIT NZ$40.6m (+16%), NPAT NZ$28.9m (+20%), EPS 14.75cps, interim DPS 10.0cps (+11%), operating cash flow NZ$38.8m (+20%), net debt reduced to NZ$17.5m (5% of total assets). Industrial EBIT +12% (constant currency +9%) on potable/wastewater and roofing/construction strength; Agri EBIT +20% on broad-based international dairy rubberware growth. Management raised FY2026 NPAT guidance to NZ$57-62m

FY2026 full-year result (year to 30 June 2026): revenue NZ$390.1m (+10%), normalised EBIT NZ$89.3m (+14-17% depending on source), normalised NPAT NZ$64.2m (+18%), reported/statutory NPAT NZ$67.7m (boosted by a NZ$4.8m pre-tax / ~NZ$3.5m post-tax non-recurring insurance gain related to the Wigram CV-line fire), operating cash flow NZ$83.6m (+26%), net debt reduced to under NZ$2m. Full-year dividend raised 18% to 30.0cps (10.0cps interim + 20.0cps final). Tenth consecutive year of record EBIT; CEO Graham Leaming stated the company had substantially offset/neutralised US tariff impacts by year-end and entered FY2027 with tariffs largely mitigated, citing pricing, cost reduction and manufacturing-mix actions; management also cited disruption from the Middle East conflict affecting sourcing during the year

Management guided to broad comfort with FY2027 consensus estimates, no material slowdown observed six weeks into FY2027, continued targeting of 11-12% compound annual EBIT/earnings growth, capex guided modestly lower than FY2026's NZ$15.1m but sustained above pre-fire historical run-rate (sub-NZ$10m), and confirmed the Wigram CV-line replacement will be installed/commissioned by end of FY2027. New China direct presence for dairy consumables and continued Netherlands/Europe build-out flagged as growth initiatives

Fonterra's Farmgate Milk Price forecast for the NZ dairy season was volatile: 2025/26 season ultimately settled at NZ$9.60-$9.80/kgMS (near-record, supportive of Agri demand), while the subsequent 2026/27 forecast was cut by Fonterra to NZ$9.25/kgMS (from an earlier $9.75 midpoint) in mid-2026 on softer global dairy prices - a watch item for Agri momentum into FY2027

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Results, 19 August 2026 (updates the interim NZ$57-62m NPAT guidance given at H1 FY2026, 11 February 2026, which itself was already achieved/exceeded by the FY2026 outcome)

items.notes: Given at H1 FY2026 (Feb 2026), raised from earlier expectations following a record first half; actual FY2026 result of NZ$64.2m normalised / $67.7m statutory NPAT exceeded the top end of this range

No explicit point-estimate range issued for FY2027 revenue/NPAT in public disclosure found; management endorsed prevailing analyst consensus on the FY2026 results call and reported no material slowdown ~6 weeks into FY2027 trading
Consistent with historical track record - Industrial EBIT CAGR of 11% and Agri EBIT CAGR of 10% over the seven years to HY26 per the company's own presentation, and EBIT 2.6x higher in FY25 than FY16

items.target: modestly below FY2026's NZ$15.1 million, but above historical sub-NZ$10 million run-rate
items.notes: Elevated partly by the Wigram CV-line replacement (fire-related) due for commissioning by end of FY2027, plus continued investment in manufacturing modernisation/flexibility

items.target: substantially offset/neutralised on a run-rate basis
items.vs_prior: improved (from an incremental cost headwind through FY25/H1 FY26)
items.notes: Management stated the ~12.5% blended tariff regime prevailing by mid-2026 is 'substantially lower' than earlier feared rates (up to 30% China / 20% Vietnam / 15% NZ scenarios flagged in FY25); timing/quantum of any tariff refunds remains uncertain and the situation is described as still capable of change

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Graham Leaming and Chair John Strowger have consistently paired record results with caution about extrapolating the run rate, citing 'global geopolitical uncertainty' and repeatedly noting that 'these record results cannot continue ad infinitum.' Nonetheless, management expressed confidence entering FY2027, citing steady early trading, continued new-product pipeline strength in both divisions, a substantially de-risked tariff position, and a very strong, low-leverage balance sheet (net debt under NZ$2m at FY2026 year-end) providing flexibility for further capacity investment and potential bolt-on M&A, while reiterating a disciplined, incremental approach to capital deployment.

bull_case: Ten consecutive years of record EBIT (FY2017-FY2026) evidences a durable, repeatable growth model built on specification lock-in, new product development and disciplined cost control - not a one-off cyclical upswing

Very low leverage (net debt fell from NZ$12.4m at FY25 year-end to under NZ$2m at FY26 year-end against a NZ$55m facility) gives Skellerup significant balance-sheet optionality for further capacity investment, in-market manufacturing expansion, or accretive bolt-on M&A without straining the dividend

Management has demonstrated it can substantially neutralise a major, well-flagged external risk (US tariffs on China/Vietnam-sourced goods) within roughly a year through pricing, cost and mix actions - reducing the probability that tariffs structurally impair future Industrial margins

Agri's dairy rubberware consumable revenue provides a relatively defensive earnings base (food-safety-driven replacement cycle) even in a softer dairy payout environment, while Industrial's potable water/wastewater exposure taps a structurally growing, less-discretionary infrastructure spending theme in the US and elsewhere

High, growing and well-covered dividend (30.0cps FY2026, +18% YoY) backed by strong operating cash flow (NZ$83.6m FY2026, +26%) appeals to income-oriented NZX investors and supports the stock's historical premium rating
bear_case: The stock trades at a premium multiple (reported trailing P/E in the high-teens to ~20x versus a ~14x average forward P/E for global machinery peers) that already prices in continued double-digit earnings growth, leaving limited margin for error if FY2027 disappoints

US tariff policy remains genuinely fluid - management itself has repeatedly cautioned that negotiated rates 'change every week,' and roughly 37-40% of group revenue is US-market exposed with ~85% of that manufactured in China/Vietnam/NZ, so a renewed escalation could reopen a material earnings headwind that has only recently been 'substantially' (not fully or permanently) offset

Fonterra's 2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast was cut to NZ$9.25/kgMS (from ~$9.75) on softening global dairy prices, a leading indicator that farmer sentiment and discretionary Agri spending (particularly footwear and equipment-adjacent products) could soften after a near-record 2025/26 payout year

FY2026's reported NPAT growth is partly flattered by a NZ$4.8m non-recurring insurance gain related to the Wigram fire; normalised NPAT growth (18%) is strong but investors should not extrapolate the statutory 24% NPAT growth (approx.) without adjusting for this one-off

Small absolute scale (~NZ$390m revenue, ~NZ$1.2bn market cap) and NZX small-cap liquidity constraints limit the pool of buyers, and the business remains exposed to lumpy single-customer events (e.g. the Health & Hygiene customer production pause that dented H1 FY26 Industrial revenue), illustrating that even a diversified 3,700-customer base cannot fully eliminate concentration risk at the margin
